analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security checks and taxes high earners and investment income to keep the program solvent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond referral, despite being backed by the Senate Budget Committee chairman and six Democratic colleagues.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have increased Social Security payments for current and future beneficiaries, raised the minimum benefit for people who worked for low wages their whole lives, and changed the inflation formula to one that tracks seniors' actual costs. To pay for it, it would have applied the Social Security payroll tax to income above $250,000 (currently capped at $147,000) and raised the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%. It never received so much as a committee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries would get larger monthly checks (an across-the-board formula boost worth roughly $2,400 a year for the average recipient, per the sponsor's framing), a cost-of-living adjustment tied to seniors' spending patterns, a new minimum benefit equal to a rising share of the poverty line for long-term low earners, and student benefits extended to age 22 for children of deceased or disabled workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and low-wage earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises benefits across the board by increasing the first bend point to 95% and applying a 22% boost to the initial benefit formula, so most retirees and disabled workers get bigger monthly checks.

Switches the cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the housing and medical costs seniors actually face, so annual increases better match their expenses.
Creates a new minimum benefit guaranteeing lifetime low earners at least a percentage of the poverty line, rising with each year worked up to 125% of the poverty level for 30 years of work.
Lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers keep collecting benefits as full-time students until age 22, instead of losing them at 19.

Pays for the expansion by applying the 12.4% payroll tax to earnings above $250,000 and raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, extending Social Security's financing into the long term.

analysis.who_pays: High earners would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages above $250,000 (the cap currently stops at $147,000), self-employed high earners would pay the same on earnings above $250,000, and wealthier households would see the net investment income tax jump from 3.8% to 16.2% on gains, dividends, and business income, with active business income newly covered.

drawbacks.text: Raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% is a steep increase on investment gains, which opponents said would reduce returns for retirees with taxable brokerage accounts and could discourage investment.

Extending the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax above $250,000 raises the cost of high earners' labor and, for self-employed professionals and business owners, their tax bill—costs that opponents argued could partly be passed along or reduce hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—higher, more inflation-protected checks for nearly every beneficiary, and a poverty-floor minimum for lifelong low earners—would be paid for by the top slice of high earners and by a large new tax on investment income. The main drawbacks are the size and reach of the investment tax (which could affect some retirement savings and incentivize shifting income) and the speed of the payroll-tax change for business owners and professionals. Critics also argued the bill asked nothing of beneficiaries in exchange, but the financing provisions were designed to more than cover the new benefits. On balance, the costs fall on a narrow, affluent group while the benefits are broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on June 9, 2022, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill had seven cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 100 senators.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll-tax cap and investors facing the higher investment-income tax keep paying the lower rates, while nothing changes for Social Security beneficiaries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors, whose taxes stay unchanged

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (VT), Chairman of the Senate Budget Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original cosponsors.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse, Jeff Merkley, Chris Van Hollen, Alex Padilla, Kirsten Gillibrand, Cory Booker

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security and tax law
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or prioritized it in 2022.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican committee majority-adjacent posture and Finance Committee leadership let it sit without action.

industries.industry: High-income professionals and self-employed business owners
industries.note: The bill would extend the 12.4% payroll tax to their earnings above $250,000, ending the cap's shelter for six-figure and seven-figure incomes.
A jump in the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, plus coverage of active business income, would sharply raise taxes on capital gains and business profits for the top households.

industries.industry: Retirees, disabled workers, and their families
industries.note: Not an industry, but the main concentrated beneficiary group: larger checks, a stronger inflation index, and a poverty-floor minimum.
